newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian crudes fall, but premiums well underpinned.
newsitem.headline: Asian crudes fall, but premiums well underpinned.

text.p: Asian crude outright prices were lower on Wednesday, but Tropical Cyclone Ophelia added to a set of already bullish factors to underpin premium levels.
Middle East grades continued to achieve premium levels for February that are 10/15 cents higher than January -- although deals for partial cargoes produced higher premiums.
Indonesian grades were well bid but mostly sold out in January, with only Minas said to be left available.
Japan utility demand and China have supported the medium type Indonesian grades, while winter demand and a widening naphtha crack have supported the lighter grades.

Cyclone Ophelia closed the offshore 80,000 barrels per day Griffin field on Tuesday but the floating production platform was making its way back to the field on Wednesday. Sources said at least five days of production could be lost by the time the field was up and running again.
There was no immediate reaction on premiums, but traders said the news added to the bullish tone for Australian grades.

North West Shelf condensate is being led by the widening naphtha crack, which stretched out to $76 per tonne earlier this month and was currently around $59 per tonne -- at the upper end of its usual range.
February Oman traded as high as MPM +28 cents, but for 140,000 barrels. Full cargoes have traded MPM +22/23 cents.

Two Murban cargoes were heard traded at ADNOC +71 and +72 cents, in line with recent deals, and a partial 300,000 barrels cargo was heard traded at +78 cents. Late deals for January Murban had traded at +65 cents.

A producer sold 200,000 barrels of Tapis to a refiner at a premium of $1.20, higher than full cargoes premiums of 90 cents to $1.00. The producer said it had a 250,000 barrel parcel left for January, but could probably muster a full cargo.
